legal.message: Since no clear law is defined, both Grendel and the Danes are guiltless evaluated from a legal perspective.

moral.message: Grendel is more guilty on the moral perspective as his killings are largely made out of the intention to cause harm, whereas the Danes mostly attack Grendel in acts of heroism or self-defense.

psychological.message: Grendel, during the 'twelve-year war' sincerely thought his killings were justified because its his purpose. He also gave humans a chance to interact with him peaceably. However, since the Danes consistently regard Grendel as a monster and attack on sight, they are psychologically more guilty.

legal.message: Whereas Grendel doesn't have a clearly defined law to defy, Frankenstein is legally guilty in witholding his culpability and is thus more legally guilty.

moral.message: Eveluated on all three ethical frameworks, Frankenstein is guilty, whereas Grendel is excused through the doctrine of double effect deontologically. Thus, Frankenstein is more morally guilty.

psychological.message: Since Frankenstein willfully abandonded the Creature, but Grendel acts according to what he thinks is his nature, Frankenstein is more psychologically guilty.

legal.message: The Creature is more legally guilty because his murders violate laws, even if he is not considered a member of the human society. Conversely, Grendel has no clearly defined laws to violate.

moral.message: The Creature is guilty according to all three ethical frameworks, where deontology partially excuses Grendel. Thus, the Creature is more morally guilty.

psychological.message: The Creature's calculated plots to exact revenge on Frankenstein demonstrate intellectual aptitude and a deep understanding of the outcome of his murders. Grendel, on the other hand, acts according to what he belives his purpose to be. Thus, the Creature is more psychologically guilty.

legal.message: Law has collapsed in both Neville and Grendel's world so both are reasonably guilt-free from a legal perspective.

moral.message: Since Neville is guiltless from a deontological perspective, whereas Grendel is only partially guiltless, Grendel is, overrall, more morally guilty.

psychological.message: Grendel is more guilty psychologically because he continues to kill even after considering that life may have meaning beyond killing (with Wealtheow). Neville's murders on the other hand come from a side of genuine self-defense and survival.

legal.message: Both Grendel and the new society are legally guilt-free.

moral.message: Grendel's murders outweigh the new society's execution of Neville on the moral scale.

psychological.message: The new society's eager anticipation to kill Neville and their sadistic excitement when killing other vampires renders them more guilty than Grendel, who only acts according to what he believes his purpose is.

legal.message: Mother is legally more guilty as her murders hold weight in Psycho's American society whereas Grendel's old society has ambiguous laws.

moral.message: Mother is more morally guilty as her murders don't achieve any net good and she relinquishes all morality when committing them. Grendel, on the other hand, can be excused in that he attempted genuine human connection at first.

psychological.message: Psychologically, Mother is more guilty as she selfishly commits murders knowing the outcome. Grendel, however, commits murders thinking that it's his purpose, which partially excuses him.

legal.message: Norman is more legally guilty as he is complicit in the murders of Mother, whereas Grendel does not have clearly defined laws to break.

moral.message: Norman bears more moral guilt as all three frameworks find him culpable in assisting with Mother's murders.

psychological.message: Since Norman is not fully in control of his mind and body, it is hard to assign him psychological guilt when, Grendel, willfully and knowingly killed the Danes.

legal.message: Marion is more legally guilty as she willfully commits theft. There are no laws to compare Grendel's murders against.

moral.message: Even though Marion checks more of the 'ethical framework boxes' compared to Grendel, the severity of her theft pales in comparison to Grendel's murders.

psychological.message: Marion is more psychologically guilty because she, in a lucid state, commits her crime and never owns up to it. Grendel, on the other hand, genuinely thinks it is his purpose to kill and acts accordingly.
